focus_relevance_note: Pre-anchor riff blueprint: Jack Bruce's descending tritone-adjacent bass riff in D, doubled by Clapton's guitar in unison, establishes the riff-first compositional contract — the riff begins before the vocal, governs the song's identity, and is the reason the song exists. The unison guitar-bass attack and the riff's low-register weight are the direct grammar that Iommi and Butler will radicalise three years later.

Pre-anchor tritone: the opening E–B-flat tritone (the diabolus in musica, the exact interval that will govern Black Sabbath's self-titled) delivered as a guitar-first motif before any vocal. Hendrix's conscious use of the devil's interval as the song's harmonic spine is the direct harmonic precursor to Iommi and Butler's tritone-first decision in 1970.

Anchor — Iommi's B–F tritone riff at funeral tempo (C# detuning from industrial accident, recorded in one day for under £500) inverts the blues-rock energy contract: the riff delivers gravitational stasis and dread rather than release. Every subsequent node in this episode is a response — inheritance, mutation, or rejection — of this weight-first aesthetic.

Immediate heir and structural expansion: the opening guitar-bass unison at half-tempo followed by a sudden speed-up is the first documented use of tempo as dramatic architecture within the weight-first contract. The 7:54 duration proves the riff-first aesthetic can sustain long-form composition — the riff governs even as the song moves through multiple tempos.

Heir via texture-as-narrative: Iommi's ring-modulated detuned power chords at 75 bpm make the guitar's sonic texture tell the story (metal man, robotic timbre). The riff is so dominant that Osbourne's vocal fits into its gaps rather than leading. First instance in the lineage where the riff's sound quality, not just its pitch content, is the compositional argument.

Speed-variant heir: the weight-first contract survives at double speed (164 bpm, written in 25 minutes as filler). No guitar solo, no bridge — the riff IS the entire musical argument. The song's UK #4 chart position proved that riff-first heavy music could be commercially dominant and radio-brief simultaneously.

Ultimate heir at maximum scale: the double-tracked E–D–C riff at 212 bpm with palm muting converts Sabbath's slow weight into kinetic weight — the riff governs eight minutes, the clean interlude (4:18–5:30) makes the riff's return a physical impact. The structural principle (riff is the song's identity) is identical to the anchor; the implementation is its thrash-metal apotheosis.

Neoclassical-harmonic mutation: Blackmore's four-note riff uses perfect fourths and a minor third rather than a tritone, generating weight through interval stacking rather than satanic dissonance. The riff-first contract is preserved (riff before vocal, riff governs identity) but the harmonic vocabulary is neoclassical rather than diabolic — the most recognisable mutation in rock history, now the first thing any beginner learns to play.

Same-era kinetic mutation: Page's A–E–A riff at 158 bpm gallops rather than pins — riff-first contract intact, but the aesthetic contract has swapped dread for momentum. Released in 1970 alongside the Black Sabbath debut, it demonstrates that the riff-first principle had two simultaneous poles from its emergence: Sabbath's slow gravity and Zeppelin's kinetic drive.

Funk-groove mutation and sub-lineage head: Perry's staccato syncopated riff swaps Sabbath's blues-minor harmonic world for James Brown's rhythmic vocabulary — the riff still governs the song but weight is delivered through rhythmic anticipation rather than low-register sustain. The 1986 Run-DMC collaboration documented the pathway from this riff's funk DNA into hip-hop, opening the sub-lineage that terminates in Killing in the Name.

Boogie-rock mutation: Young's E–D–A major-key riff at 96 bpm uses Chuck Berry's shuffle rather than minor-scale darkness — weight delivered through rhythmic inevitability and dynamic anticipation. The most commercially successful mutation (estimated 50 million copies sold), proving the riff-first principle could dominate without harmonic dread and replacing Sabbath's supernatural fear with post-Bon Scott resilience.

Neoclassical vocabulary mutation: Rhoads' A–F#–D riff uses diminished and chromatic movement from 18th-century European classical music rather than tritone dissonance or blues. The riff still governs the song — Rhoads conceived it as a compositional theme first — but the harmonic language is Bach filtered through Marshall distortion. Rhoads' documented UCLA-trained intention to apply counterpoint to rock makes this the most intellectually self-aware mutation in the lineage.

Terminal node of the funk-groove sub-lineage: Morello's two-note riff with whammy-bar noise descends methodologically from Walk This Way's syncopated staccato approach, combined with hip-hop rhythm. The riff is now a political weapon rather than an aesthetic — the lyric's repeated F-word climax functions as a riff in itself. The methodological_descent path Walk This Way → Killing in the Name is the episode's alternative mutation axis.

Commercial-simplification mutation: Hammett's E–F#–E–G power-chord riff at 123 bpm is the most accessible distillation of Sabbath's weight-first contract — slow, repetitive, immediately memorable — but with tritone dissonance replaced by a major-key power chord sequence. The Black Album's 16+ million US sales are the commercial zenith of the riff-first principle, reached precisely as grunge (Come As You Are, released the same month) begins its inversion.

First inversion of the weight-first contract: Slash's arpeggiated D–C#–A–G single-note arpeggio figure prioritises lyrical tenderness over weight. The riff still governs (the opening arpeggio is more famous than the chorus) but the aesthetic goal has inverted: instead of dread or force, the riff delivers nostalgia and beauty. Slash has described writing it as a 'circus melody' — the deliberate lightness is the mutation's defining act.

Texture-inversion: the riff uses the same interval vocabulary as Enter Sandman but played through a Boss CE-2 chorus pedal, converting metal weight into underwater drift. Released the same month as the Black Album, it is grunge's direct answer to metal's commercial zenith — riff-first structure retained, weight aesthetic explicitly rejected through Cobain's documented intention to 'feminise' the hard rock template.

Harmonic-register inversion: Thayil's G–E–Eb–Bb–Ab progression in drop D uses Sabbath's detuning and Sabbath's funeral tempo (73 bpm) but refuses the minor-key darkness — major-key lush harmony delivers surreal beauty instead of dread through the same sonic weight. The inversion mechanism is tonal: equal heaviness, opposite emotional destination.

Closing inversion and loop-back: White's five-note descending motif (played on guitar through an octave pedal simulating bass) is a single-instrument minimal figure that paradoxically echoes the anchor's own minimalism — both songs use a descending low-register motif as sole compositional argument. Where Sabbath uses two instruments to create maximum weight, White uses one instrument pretending to be two to create the same riff-first impact from minimum forces. The loop-back to the anchor's motif while rejecting its weight aesthetic is the episode's closing argument.
